Inside TIJCEF’s School Takeover Day: Staff, Volunteers Lead Full-Day Learning in Yola

Inside TIJCEF’s School Takeover Day: Staff, Volunteers Lead Full-Day Learning in Yola

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) has taken its education intervention beyond the conventional model of brief school visits by deploying its staff and volunteers to a community school in Yola, Adamawa State, where they spent an entire school day participating in and supporting learning activities from the opening period until closing time.

The intervention formed part of TIJCEF’s School Takeover Day, a recurring programme conducted twice each year in which the Foundation selects a school and mobilises staff and volunteers to spend a full day working within the school environment.

Rather than arriving for a short motivational talk, presentation or ceremonial visit, the TIJCEF team participates in the school’s activities throughout the day. Staff and volunteers interact with pupils, support classroom learning and work alongside members of the school community until the end of the school day.

Photographs from the Yola edition document both classroom and wider school engagement. In one of the classroom sessions, pupils can be seen participating in an interactive numerical exercise while a TIJCEF team member guides the activity. Other photographs show children, school personnel and members of the Foundation together within the school premises.

The programme represents TIJCEF’s attempt to make community education support more participatory: instead of observing a school from outside, its team enters the learning environment and experiences a full school day alongside the pupils and teachers.

From School Visit to Full-Day Participation

School outreaches by civil society organisations can sometimes last only a few hours. Visitors arrive, address pupils, distribute materials, take photographs and leave.

TIJCEF’s School Takeover Day uses a different model.

For the selected day, staff and volunteers commit themselves to the school from the beginning of activities through the closing period.

This extended presence allows the Foundation to engage pupils in a setting closer to their normal learning experience.

The programme is not intended to permanently replace qualified teachers or school administrators. Instead, it provides a designated day during which TIJCEF personnel and volunteers contribute their time, knowledge and energy to supporting school activities and engaging directly with children.

Conducting the programme twice annually also distinguishes it from an isolated outreach.

Each edition becomes another opportunity for the Foundation to take its education work into a school environment and develop practical experience that can inform subsequent interventions.

Learning Takes Centre Stage

The Yola edition demonstrated the educational character of the programme.

Classroom photographs show pupils actively participating rather than sitting through a ceremonial presentation.

Children held handwritten learning materials while a TIJCEF team member facilitated an interactive exercise. The classroom board and materials visible during the activity further document that the engagement took place within an active learning setting.

That distinction is important.

TIJCEF’s involvement was not limited to gathering pupils for photographs. The team participated in activities during the school day.

Interactive engagement can also provide volunteers with a closer understanding of how children respond to different approaches to learning.

Some children may respond quickly to verbal questions. Others may participate more confidently when learning involves physical objects, group interaction or visual materials.

Spending a full day within the school gives volunteers greater exposure to these differences than would normally be possible during a brief visit.

Nigeria’s Foundational Learning Challenge Gives the Programme Wider Relevance

TIJCEF’s intervention comes against the background of a serious learning challenge facing Nigerian children.

UNICEF has warned that Nigeria faces a severe foundational learning crisis, reporting that more than 70 per cent of children lack foundational literacy and numeracy skills. The organisation has highlighted teacher capacity, learning resources and the quality of instruction among issues requiring sustained attention. UNICEF Nigeria – Enabling Teachers, Educating Children⁠�

That national statistic should not be interpreted as an assessment of the pupils involved in TIJCEF’s Yola programme.

No learning assessment from the School Takeover Day has been presented to establish the literacy or numeracy performance of participating pupils.

Instead, the national evidence provides context for why initiatives that bring additional attention to children’s learning remain relevant.

TIJCEF’s programme cannot solve Nigeria’s foundational learning crisis, nor is a twice-yearly intervention a substitute for sustained classroom teaching.

Its contribution is much more specific: mobilising people and resources to spend a full school day supporting learning and engaging directly with a school community.

Teachers Remain Central to Education

The School Takeover Day also provides an opportunity to recognise rather than diminish the role of teachers.

Teachers perform this work every school day.

What TIJCEF staff and volunteers experience for a single day is part of the daily responsibility carried by educators throughout the academic year.

The intervention can therefore provide civil society volunteers with greater appreciation of the realities of classroom management and teaching.

UNESCO estimates that the world will need 44 million additional primary and secondary teachers by 2030 to meet universal education goals, illustrating the importance of teachers to the global education system. UNESCO – Global Report on Teachers⁠�

The TIJCEF programme should consequently be understood as support for education, not substitution for professional educators.

Volunteers Move From Observers to Participants

The School Takeover Day also gives TIJCEF volunteers a practical role.

Volunteerism can easily become symbolic when participants are present only during opening ceremonies or photographs.

A full-day model requires more.

Volunteers have to interact with pupils.

They have to participate in activities.

They experience the rhythm of a school day.

They also have an opportunity to observe some of the practical realities affecting learning within a community-school environment.

That experience can be valuable to TIJCEF itself.

Community organisations make stronger programme decisions when they understand the environments in which beneficiaries live and learn.

A photograph or written report can communicate some information about a school.

Spending a complete day there can provide a different level of exposure.

Twice a Year Creates Opportunity for Better Measurement

Because TIJCEF conducts the School Takeover Day twice annually, the programme also presents an opportunity to strengthen the Foundation’s evidence-based approach.

Each edition can be documented using a consistent framework.

TIJCEF can record the school selected, number of pupils directly participating, number of staff and volunteers deployed, subjects or activities supported, duration of engagement and feedback from teachers and pupils.

Where appropriate, short learning assessments could also be introduced.

For example, if an edition includes a specific numeracy activity, a simple exercise administered before and after the session could provide evidence about immediate learning.

The Foundation should not manufacture improvement percentages in advance.

Results should come from actual assessments.

Over several editions, such records could transform School Takeover Day from a recurring volunteer activity into a programme with an increasingly strong evidence base.

A Programme That Can Travel Beyond One School

Another strength of the model is its potential flexibility.

Because School Takeover Day is based on mobilising staff and volunteers around a selected school, future editions can reach different communities.

This allows TIJCEF to take the programme to schools where engagement could be particularly valuable rather than concentrating every edition in one institution.

The twice-yearly structure can also create continuity without requiring TIJCEF to claim that it operates the schools involved.

The Foundation comes in for a defined intervention, works with the existing school community and completes the edition at the end of the school day.

The school remains under its normal administration.

This distinction is important when describing the term “takeover.”

TIJCEF is not assuming administrative ownership or control of a school. School Takeover Day is the programme concept used to describe a full-day intervention in which TIJCEF’s staff and volunteers immerse themselves in school activities from opening until closing.

Supporting SDG 4 at Grassroots Level

The programme also aligns with the broader objectives of Sustainable Development Goal 4, which seeks inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning opportunities.

Among its targets are improvements in access to education and the acquisition of relevant learning outcomes. United Nations – Sustainable Development Goal 4⁠�

TIJCEF’s contribution is necessarily local.

A community organisation cannot achieve a national or global education target through a single programme.

But global development objectives ultimately have to translate into activities affecting real people in real communities.

For TIJCEF, School Takeover Day provides one mechanism for making that connection.

More Than a Photograph

The images emerging from the Yola programme tell two complementary stories.

The group photograph documents the relationship between TIJCEF personnel, school representatives and pupils.

The classroom photograph goes further by showing the programme in action.

It captures children participating in an educational exercise while a member of the TIJCEF team facilitates the activity.

That second image is particularly important because it demonstrates what distinguishes School Takeover Day from an ordinary courtesy visit.

The Foundation was not simply present at the school.

Its people were participating in the school day.

From Opening Bell to Closing Time

The defining feature of TIJCEF’s School Takeover Day is ultimately its duration and level of participation.

The team arrives for the start of the school day.

Staff and volunteers engage with the school community.

They participate in learning and other activities.

And they remain through the closing period.

Then, later in the year, the programme happens again.

That twice-yearly commitment gives TIJCEF an opportunity to develop School Takeover Day into a recognisable part of its education portfolio while progressively improving how each edition is documented and evaluated.

The Yola intervention demonstrates what the concept looks like in practice: TIJCEF staff and volunteers leaving their normal routines for a day and entering the everyday learning environment of children.

It does not replace teachers.

It does not claim to solve Nigeria’s education challenges in a day.

And it should not be measured merely by photographs taken or hours spent at a school.

Its value lies in direct participation—bringing volunteers, children and educators together for a full school day centred on learning, engagement and community service.

For the pupils involved, it is a different kind of school day.

For TIJCEF staff and volunteers, it is an opportunity to serve from inside the classroom rather than from a distance.

And for the Foundation, the twice-yearly programme provides a practical expression of its commitment to taking community development directly to the places where children learn, interact and prepare for their future.

TIJCEF Strengthens Evidence-Based Programming Through Monitoring and Impact Documentation

TIJCEF Strengthens Evidence-Based Programming Through Monitoring and Impact Documentation

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) is strengthening its approach to community development by placing programme documentation, beneficiary records and measurable results at the centre of how it tracks and communicates its interventions across communities.

The approach forms part of TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar, one of the four pillars guiding the Foundation’s work alongside Dignity, Agency and Resilience.

Rather than relying solely on statements about people being “empowered” or “impacted,” TIJCEF’s evidence approach focuses on documenting what interventions were implemented, where they took place, who participated, how many direct beneficiaries were reached and what programme records are available to support reported results.

The importance of this approach can already be seen across TIJCEF’s programme portfolio.

At Adroit International Academy in Yola, TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation implemented a girls’ empowerment intervention reaching 200 girls.

At Government Girls College Yola, more than 400 girls participated in a STEM-focused outreach.

A youth empowerment seminar at Zion Centre in Girei reached 50 young people, while a women’s leadership and empowerment intervention in Taraba State reached 45 women.

These programme-level figures provide TIJCEF with something more valuable than general claims about community impact: identifiable records connecting beneficiaries to specific interventions.

From Activities to Verifiable Programme Records

Grassroots organisations frequently work in environments where immediate community needs take priority over sophisticated data systems.

A programme may be successfully conducted and photographed, but important information can be lost if beneficiary numbers, locations, dates, activities and outcomes are not properly recorded.

TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar seeks to address this challenge by treating documentation as part of programme implementation rather than an activity that begins only when an annual report or funding proposal is required.

This means evidence can begin with relatively simple records.

How many people attended?

Where did the programme take place?

Who were the implementing partners?

What group was targeted?

What activities were delivered?

What materials were provided?

What photographs, attendance records or participant feedback exist?

These questions help turn an activity into a documented intervention.

Programme Figures Show Different Levels of Reach

TIJCEF’s existing programme records illustrate why intervention-level documentation matters.

The Foundation should not simply combine every number into a large headline figure without retaining information about where those beneficiaries came from.

For example, the 200 girls reached at Adroit International Academy can be linked to a specific school-based girls’ empowerment programme jointly implemented with Lead the Girl Foundation.

The 400-plus girls reached at Government Girls College Yola belong to a different intervention focused on STEM exposure.

The 50 young people reached at Zion Centre, Girei, represent participants in a youth empowerment seminar.

The 45 women reached through the Taraba leadership and empowerment programme represent another distinct beneficiary group.

Separating these records allows TIJCEF to understand not only how many people it reaches but who it is reaching and through what type of intervention.

That is a more useful measure for programme management.

Evidence Prevents Double Counting

Maintaining programme-level records also helps prevent a common problem in development reporting: double counting.

A person may participate in more than one programme.

For example, an individual who attends a leadership programme could later volunteer during another TIJCEF intervention.

If every attendance is automatically counted as a unique beneficiary, the organisation’s cumulative reach could become inflated.

An evidence-based system should therefore distinguish between programme participations and unique beneficiaries wherever records make that possible.

The distinction becomes increasingly important as TIJCEF expands.

Programme participation tells the Foundation how much activity it has delivered.

Unique-beneficiary data provide a better indication of how many individual people have actually been reached.

Both measurements can be useful, but they answer different questions.

Evidence Also Means Acknowledging What Is Not Known

TIJCEF’s approach to evidence is equally important when programme information is incomplete.

The Foundation’s 2023 outreach to an orphanage in Katsina, for instance, can be documented through the visit by its Executive Director and the donation of gifts to children.

However, where a verified beneficiary figure is not available, an estimated number should not be introduced simply to make the programme appear larger.

Similarly, TIJCEF’s January 2026 two-day leadership training can be reported through its duration, programme records and participation of the President of Public Speakers Network of Africa Foundation alongside other resource persons.

Where the exact attendance figure has not been verified, it is more credible to leave that figure unstated than to estimate it.

This principle is central to evidence-based reporting:

What is not measured should not be presented as measured.

That standard protects both beneficiaries and the organisation.

Photographs Form Part of the Evidence Base

Programme photography also plays an important role in TIJCEF’s documentation.

Images from training sessions, school programmes and community activities provide visual records showing how interventions were implemented.

They can document participation, programme settings, organisational branding and engagement between volunteers, resource persons and beneficiaries.

But photographs have limitations.

A photograph showing a crowded training hall cannot independently establish that 100 people attended.

A photograph of smiling participants cannot prove that their income increased.

A picture of students during a STEM outreach cannot establish that they subsequently pursued STEM careers.

Photography therefore supports evidence but does not replace beneficiary records or outcome measurement.

This distinction enables TIJCEF to use visual documentation responsibly.

Beneficiary Numbers Are Outputs, Not Automatically Impact

One of the most important elements of the Evidence pillar is distinguishing between outputs and outcomes.

Reaching 400 girls is an output.

Showing that those girls increased their STEM knowledge would be an outcome.

Training 50 young people is an output.

Showing that participants subsequently applied specific skills would represent a further result.

Reaching 45 women through leadership programming is an output.

Demonstrating increased participation in leadership or livelihood activities would require additional evidence.

This distinction prevents programme reach from automatically being described as transformation.

TIJCEF can celebrate beneficiary numbers while remaining accurate about what those figures actually demonstrate.

Evidence Supports Sustainable Development

TIJCEF’s approach also connects with the wider international emphasis on data in sustainable development.

The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal framework relies heavily on indicators because progress cannot be assessed effectively without reliable information.

SDG 17, for example, includes targets related to increasing the availability of high-quality, timely and reliable data for sustainable development. United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 17⁠�

For a grassroots organisation, this does not require building a national statistical system.

It begins with ensuring that programme information is recorded consistently.

A reliable attendance sheet is evidence.

A properly completed beneficiary questionnaire is evidence.

A dated programme photograph is evidence.

A partner confirmation is evidence.

A pre- and post-programme assessment can provide evidence of change.

A follow-up interview can provide evidence about what happened after an intervention.

When combined systematically, these records create an increasingly strong picture of organisational performance.

Evidence Strengthens Accountability to Partners

Good programme data are also important for partnerships and fundraising.

Potential donors and institutional partners increasingly expect organisations to demonstrate what they have previously implemented.

An organisation able to provide programme dates, locations, beneficiary numbers, photographs, partners and measurable results is better positioned to demonstrate institutional capacity than one relying exclusively on broad statements.

For TIJCEF, this means its programme history can become part of its organisational evidence base.

The Adroit intervention demonstrates collaboration with another foundation.

The Government Girls College programme demonstrates large-scale school engagement.

The Girei seminar demonstrates youth-focused programming.

The Taraba intervention provides evidence of women-focused engagement.

The volunteer training demonstrates investment in internal capacity.

And the Katsina outreach documents humanitarian engagement with vulnerable children.

Together, these interventions begin to establish a traceable record of what the Foundation has done.

Evidence Must Protect Beneficiaries

Collecting information also creates responsibilities.

TIJCEF’s programmes involve groups including children and young people, meaning data collection must respect privacy, dignity and safeguarding principles.

Not every piece of information collected should be published.

Beneficiary names, contact information and sensitive personal details should be handled carefully.

Public impact reporting can rely primarily on aggregated information.

Instead of identifying individual children, TIJCEF can report that 200 girls participated in a programme.

Instead of publishing private questionnaire responses, results can be presented as aggregated percentages where appropriate.

This allows evidence to strengthen accountability without compromising beneficiary dignity.

Building a Culture of Evidence

TIJCEF’s Evidence pillar ultimately goes beyond numbers.

It represents an organisational culture in which claims are expected to have supporting records.

That means being willing to report both achievements and limitations.

It means distinguishing between direct beneficiaries and estimated reach.

It means recognising partners rather than claiming collaborative programmes as exclusively TIJCEF interventions.

It means acknowledging when a beneficiary number is unavailable.

And it means avoiding impressive-looking percentages that have no underlying dataset.

For a growing grassroots organisation, these practices can become important institutional strengths.

TIJCEF’s programmes already provide the foundation.

There are documented interventions involving 200 girls at Adroit International Academy, more than 400 girls at Government Girls College Yola, 50 young people in Girei and 45 women in Taraba, alongside other activities for which different forms of programme evidence exist.

The task of the Evidence pillar is to ensure that those activities become more than memories or photographs.

They become records.

Those records become data.

And where appropriate measurement exists, that data can eventually demonstrate outcomes.

For TIJCEF, this is what evidence-based community development means: not merely saying that impact happened, but building the records capable of showing what was done, who was reached and what changed.

TIJCEF Strengthens Community Resilience Through Volunteer Training in Yola

TIJCEF Strengthens Community Resilience Through Volunteer Training in Yola

 

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) strengthened its community-development capacity in April 2026 through a volunteer training programme in Yola, Adamawa State, bringing volunteers together to improve their preparedness for community service and the implementation of the Foundation’s grassroots interventions.

 

The training formed part of TIJCEF’s efforts to build a stronger network of people capable of supporting programmes involving women, girls, young people and vulnerable communities.

 

Rather than focusing exclusively on beneficiaries, the programme turned attention to an important group behind successful community interventions: volunteers.

 

For TIJCEF, volunteers provide a connection between organisational plans and the communities in which programmes are implemented. Their ability to communicate, work with beneficiaries, understand programme objectives and represent the organisation responsibly can influence the quality of interventions delivered in the field.

 

The Yola training therefore falls under TIJCEF’s Resilience pillar, reflecting the Foundation’s recognition that sustainable community action requires organisations themselves to develop people, structures and systems capable of continuing their work in changing circumstances.

 

Training Volunteers for Community Service

 

The April 2026 programme was organised as a capacity-building intervention for TIJCEF volunteers.

 

The training provided an opportunity to bring individuals involved in the Foundation’s activities together within a structured learning environment.

 

For a grassroots organisation, this type of internal capacity development is important.

 

Community programmes may be carefully designed at organisational level, but implementation frequently depends on people working directly with beneficiaries.

 

Volunteers can support registration.

 

They can assist with programme coordination.

 

They can communicate with participants.

 

They can help distribute materials.

 

They can support documentation.

 

They may also represent the Foundation during interactions with schools, community leaders and other stakeholders.

 

Training therefore provides an opportunity to strengthen how these responsibilities are carried out.

 

TIJCEF’s decision to invest in volunteer development in Yola demonstrates that the Foundation’s community work is not limited to organising public-facing programmes.

 

It also includes building the human capacity required to deliver those programmes.

 

Volunteers Play an Important Role in Development

 

Volunteerism contributes significantly to community development around the world.

 

The United Nations Volunteers programme describes volunteerism as an important mechanism through which people participate in development and contribute to their communities.

 

The 2022 State of the World’s Volunteerism Report estimated that approximately 862 million people aged 15 and above volunteer globally each month, demonstrating the scale at which voluntary action contributes to societies. “United Nations Volunteers – State of the World’s Volunteerism Report” (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/0)

 

The global figure is not presented as a measure of TIJCEF’s volunteer network.

 

Instead, it demonstrates the broader importance of voluntary service as a component of development.

 

At community level, volunteers can help organisations extend their activities beyond what paid staff alone may be able to accomplish.

 

This can be particularly important for grassroots organisations operating with limited financial and human resources.

 

Building Resilience Within the Organisation

 

TIJCEF’s Resilience pillar is often expressed through programmes designed to strengthen beneficiaries’ capacity to respond to social and economic challenges.

 

The volunteer training represents another side of resilience: organisational resilience.

 

An organisation becomes more resilient when knowledge and responsibility are distributed among multiple people rather than concentrated in a small leadership team.

 

If only one or two individuals understand how programmes are organised, activities can become difficult to sustain when those individuals are unavailable.

 

Training volunteers expands the number of people who understand the organisation’s work and can contribute to programme implementation.

 

This can strengthen continuity.

 

It can also improve the Foundation’s ability to respond when new opportunities or community needs arise.

 

The April training therefore served not only the individuals participating but also TIJCEF’s wider programme structure.

 

Supporting TIJCEF’s Growing Programme Activities

 

The volunteer training came during a period of expanding activity for the Foundation.

 

TIJCEF’s interventions have involved different beneficiary groups and programme settings, from girls’ empowerment in schools to leadership programmes, women’s empowerment and youth-focused activities.

 

Each type of programme creates different logistical and human-resource demands.

 

A school outreach involving hundreds of girls requires coordination.

 

A leadership training programme requires participant management and documentation.

 

A community intervention may require mobilisation and communication with local stakeholders.

 

Humanitarian activities can require careful handling and distribution of materials.

 

Volunteers can support these processes when they understand their responsibilities.

 

Training therefore becomes part of programme quality rather than an activity separate from programme delivery.

 

Community Engagement Requires Responsibility

 

Working with communities also creates responsibilities.

 

Volunteers may encounter children, women or other people in vulnerable situations.

 

How volunteers communicate with participants and handle personal information can affect the dignity and safety of beneficiaries.

 

This is especially important when programmes involve children.

 

TIJCEF’s activities involving girls and other young people require attention to appropriate safeguarding and responsible documentation.

 

Photographs, names and personal information should be handled carefully.

 

Volunteers representing the Foundation also need to understand that their conduct can influence public trust in the organisation.

 

A poorly managed interaction can damage a relationship with a school or community.

 

Professional and respectful engagement can strengthen that relationship.

 

Capacity development therefore contributes to more than operational efficiency. It can help establish common expectations regarding how an organisation interacts with the people it serves.

 

Volunteer Development Supports the SDGs

 

Volunteerism also has a recognised relationship with the Sustainable Development Goals.

 

The United Nations has highlighted the role volunteers can play in implementing development initiatives and strengthening people’s participation in sustainable development.

 

For TIJCEF, this connection is practical.

 

Its community programmes already intersect with development areas such as gender equality, education, health, youth development and community wellbeing.

 

Volunteers can contribute to these interventions through mobilisation, programme support, communication and documentation.

 

Building their capacity can therefore strengthen the Foundation’s ability to contribute at grassroots level to wider development objectives.

 

The scale of TIJCEF’s contribution remains local, but local action forms part of the broader development process.

 

Training as an Investment in People

 

Volunteer training also provides value to the volunteers themselves.

 

People who participate in community service can gain exposure to programme organisation, teamwork, communication and social-development activities.

 

For young volunteers in particular, these experiences can complement formal education.

 

However, TIJCEF should distinguish between providing exposure and claiming outcomes that have not been measured.

 

Participation in a volunteer training programme does not automatically prove that every participant acquired employment or developed a specific level of professional competence.

 

The documented result is that TIJCEF conducted the training in Yola in April 2026 as part of its volunteer-capacity development.

 

Any specific claims about knowledge improvement or subsequent professional outcomes would require supporting assessment or follow-up evidence.

 

Strengthening the People Behind the Programmes

 

The Yola training is significant because impact organisations are often judged almost entirely by the number of external beneficiaries they reach.

 

Those figures are important, but they do not tell the entire story.

 

Behind every well-organised intervention are people responsible for planning, mobilisation, logistics, communication and documentation.

 

For TIJCEF, volunteers form part of that structure.

 

Investing in them is therefore an investment in the Foundation’s capacity to serve communities effectively.

 

The programme also demonstrates why resilience must be built internally as well as externally.

 

An organisation that seeks to strengthen communities must itself develop systems and people capable of sustaining its work.

 

Building a Stronger Foundation for Community Impact

 

TIJCEF’s April 2026 volunteer training in Yola represents a documented step towards strengthening that internal capacity.

 

The programme brought volunteers together.

 

It focused on preparing people involved in the Foundation’s community work.

 

And it strengthened the human network supporting TIJCEF’s expanding interventions.

 

Unlike the Girei youth empowerment seminar, which directly focused on young beneficiaries, the Yola volunteer programme concentrated on people helping the Foundation deliver its mission.

 

This makes the two Resilience interventions fundamentally different.

 

One seeks to strengthen the resilience of young people facing social and economic challenges.

 

The other strengthens the organisational and volunteer capacity required to continue serving communities.

 

Together, they demonstrate the two sides of resilience reflected in TIJCEF’s work: building stronger people in communities and building a stronger organisation capable of standing with those communities.

 

As TIJCEF continues expanding its programmes, trained and committed volunteers will remain important to translating plans into action.

 

The April 2026 Yola programme therefore represents more than an internal meeting.

 

It forms part of the infrastructure behind TIJCEF’s community impact the people who help move the Foundation’s mission from organisational objectives to practical service on the ground.

TIJCEF Builds Youth Resilience Through Empowerment Seminar in Girei

TIJCEF Builds Youth Resilience Through Empowerment Seminar in Girei

 

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) has strengthened its youth-development interventions in Adamawa State through an empowerment seminar held at Zion Centre in Girei, bringing together 50 young people for an engagement focused on personal development, empowerment and building capacity to navigate social and economic challenges.

 

The programme directly reached 50 participants, providing TIJCEF with a documented beneficiary figure for the intervention and adding to the Foundation’s growing portfolio of youth-focused activities.

 

Unlike TIJCEF’s girls’ empowerment programme at Adroit International Academy or its women-focused intervention in Taraba State, the Girei programme was designed specifically around young people and the importance of strengthening their capacity to respond to challenges, recognise opportunities and contribute positively to their communities.

 

The intervention falls under TIJCEF’s Resilience pillar, which focuses on helping individuals and communities develop the capacity to withstand challenges, adapt to changing circumstances and pursue opportunities despite social and economic pressures.

 

The Girei seminar was implemented against a wider national environment in which Nigerian youths continue to confront employment difficulties, skills gaps, economic pressures and uncertainty about pathways from education into sustainable livelihoods.

 

50 Young People Reached in Girei

 

According to TIJCEF’s programme records, 50 young people participated in the seminar at Zion Centre, Girei.

 

The figure represents direct programme participation and is not an estimate based on indirect reach.

 

For TIJCEF, working with a defined group of 50 participants provided an opportunity to bring young people together within a structured setting for an empowerment-focused engagement.

 

The programme reflected the Foundation’s belief that resilience cannot be built through material support alone.

 

Young people also require access to knowledge, exposure, networks and opportunities that can strengthen their ability to respond to changing circumstances.

 

This is particularly relevant in a country where the transition between education and employment can be difficult for many young people.

 

Youth Development Remains a Major Nigerian Challenge

 

Nigeria’s demographic structure makes youth development a national priority.

 

With a large and youthful population, the country’s ability to provide young people with education, skills and pathways into productive economic activity has major implications for future development.

 

Nigeria’s National Employment Policy 2025 recognises some of these challenges.

 

The International Labour Organization reported that the policy seeks to respond to unemployment and underemployment while strengthening employment creation, skills development, youth participation and inclusive economic opportunities.

 

The policy also places emphasis on preparing Nigerians for changes in the labour market and improving the relationship between skills development and employment opportunities. “International Labour Organization – Nigeria National Employment Policy 2025” (https://reference-url-citation.invalid/0)

 

TIJCEF’s Girei intervention operates at a much smaller scale than national employment programmes.

 

However, grassroots programmes have a different role.

 

They can engage young people directly within their communities and create opportunities for interaction that may be difficult to achieve through large national programmes alone.

 

The 50 participants reached in Girei represent this community-level approach.

 

Resilience Means Preparing for Challenges

 

TIJCEF’s classification of the programme under its Resilience pillar reflects the nature of the intervention.

 

Resilience is sometimes associated primarily with natural disasters or humanitarian emergencies.

 

For young people, however, resilience can also involve the ability to respond constructively to unemployment, economic difficulties, educational setbacks and other challenges encountered during the transition into adulthood.

 

This does not mean young people should simply be expected to endure difficult economic conditions.

 

Structural challenges require government policies, investment, employment creation and functioning public institutions.

 

At the individual level, however, knowledge, adaptability and access to opportunities can influence how people respond when difficulties arise.

 

Youth empowerment programmes can contribute to this capacity.

 

The Girei seminar therefore provided TIJCEF with a platform to engage 50 young people around personal development and empowerment within their local environment.

 

Economic Conditions Give the Programme Wider Relevance

 

Nigeria’s poverty situation provides additional context for grassroots resilience programmes.

These relationships show why community problems should not always be treated in isolation. A girl’s ability to participate confidently in school may depend on access to menstrual-health information, suitable materials, clean water, safe toilets, supportive teachers and a school culture free from stigma.

TIJCEF’s Four-Pillar Approach

TIJCEF organises its work around four programme pillars: Dignity, Agency, Resilience and Evidence.

Dignity focuses on menstrual health, WASH, safety and the well-being of women and girls. Agency promotes education, leadership, mentoring, life skills and opportunities that help people make informed decisions. Resilience addresses climate education, environmental responsibility and community preparedness. Evidence strengthens research, geospatial analysis, monitoring, evaluation and advocacy.

Together, the pillars provide a framework through which TIJCEF can connect immediate community needs with long-term development.

For example, distributing menstrual materials may respond to an urgent need, but sustainable menstrual dignity also requires education, functional sanitation facilities, supportive policies, responsible waste management and reliable evidence about the challenges girls experience.

International visibility creates both opportunities and responsibilities. As more people discover TIJCEF through public platforms, the organisation must continue strengthening its governance, documentation, safeguarding and financial accountability.

TIJCEF recognises that credibility is built through consistent action, honest reporting and respect for the people it serves. Programme figures should be supported by attendance records and activity reports. Photographs and beneficiary stories should be used with appropriate consent. Financial contributions should be documented and applied responsibly.

The Foundation’s Evidence pillar is important to this commitment. Monitoring and evaluation help TIJCEF understand whether activities are reaching intended participants and producing useful results. Evidence also enables the organisation to acknowledge limitations, document lessons and improve future interventions.

An Opportunity for Stronger Partnerships

The United Nations platform listing can make it easier for potential partners, donors, researchers and development organisations to discover TIJCEF’s work. However, meaningful partnerships require more than online visibility.

TIJCEF seeks partnerships that respect local knowledge, strengthen organisational capacity and produce measurable benefits for communities. Schools can provide access to students and support follow-up activities. Health professionals can contribute technical knowledge. Researchers can strengthen programme design and evaluation. Businesses can provide materials, technology and financial support.

Local leaders and community members are equally important because they understand the social realities that shape participation and sustainability.

Looking Ahead

TIJCEF’s inclusion on the United Nations SDG Partnerships Platform is a meaningful step in the Foundation’s development. It places a community-driven Nigerian organisation within a global conversation about sustainable development and highlights the importance of locally led action.

The milestone does not mark the completion of TIJCEF’s mission. Instead, it creates a stronger obligation to deepen impact, improve accountability and expand effective programmes responsibly.

TIJCEF will continue working with women, girls, young people, volunteers, schools and community stakeholders to advance dignity, strengthen agency, build resilience and generate evidence for lasting change.

TIJCEF Completes STEM Empowerment Project, Reaches 400 Girls in Yola

 

Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF) successfully completed its STEM Empowerment Project on 23 February 2026 at Government Girls’ School, Yola, Adamawa State. The completed intervention reached 400 girls and strengthened their exposure to science, technology, engineering and mathematics as pathways to education, innovation, leadership and future economic opportunities.

 

The project was implemented under TIJCEF’s Agency Pillar, which focuses on enabling women and girls to develop the knowledge, confidence, skills and opportunities required to make informed choices and shape their own futures.

 

Rather than viewing the participating students only as beneficiaries, the initiative recognised them as individuals with ideas, ambitions and the capacity to contribute meaningfully to their communities. It encouraged the girls to see themselves as potential scientists, engineers, healthcare professionals, surveyors, researchers, environmental specialists, technology entrepreneurs and leaders.

 

Building Agency Through STEM Education

 

For TIJCEF, agency means more than giving assistance to women and girls. It involves creating opportunities that allow them to recognise their abilities, express their ideas, make informed decisions and pursue their aspirations without being restricted by gender stereotypes or limited exposure.

 

The STEM Empowerment Project reflected this commitment by introducing 400 girls to the possibilities available within science and technology-related fields. It was designed to strengthen their confidence and encourage them to approach STEM subjects as areas in which they could participate, grow and succeed.

 

Science, technology, engineering and mathematics are not simply academic subjects. They help young people develop curiosity, creativity, critical thinking and problem-solving abilities. These skills can support girls in making better decisions, responding to challenges and developing solutions that benefit their schools, families and communities.

 

By bringing the intervention directly to Government Girls’ School, Yola, TIJCEF created an opportunity to engage the students within their learning environment. Schools are important spaces for building agency because the encouragement girls receive during their formative years can influence their educational choices, professional ambitions and willingness to take on leadership responsibilities.

 

Helping Girls See New Possibilities

 

Many girls have the ability to succeed in STEM but may not always receive the exposure, encouragement or opportunities needed to develop their interests. Social expectations and gender stereotypes can sometimes create the impression that technical and scientific fields are more suitable for boys.

 

Limited access to role models and relevant learning opportunities can also affect how girls perceive their abilities and available career options. When these barriers are not addressed, talented girls may abandon their interests or avoid subjects and professions they are fully capable of pursuing.

 

TIJCEF’s STEM Empowerment Project helped challenge these limitations by encouraging the participating girls to recognise that their gender does not determine their intelligence, potential or professional future.

 

The initiative promoted a simple but important message: girls have the right and ability to learn, innovate, lead and contribute to technological and scientific development.

 

This message is central to the Agency Pillar. A girl who believes in her ability to learn is more likely to ask questions, explore opportunities and make informed decisions about her education. She is also better positioned to resist limiting stereotypes and pursue a future based on her interests and abilities.

 

From Beneficiaries to Future Problem-Solvers

 

TIJCEF believes that girls should not only receive support but should also be equipped to become active problem-solvers and decision-makers.

 

The 400 girls reached through the completed project represent 400 individual ambitions with the potential to influence families, communities and institutions. Each participant has the capacity to use knowledge and confidence gained through educational opportunities to contribute to society.

 

A girl encouraged to pursue STEM today may become an engineer who designs essential infrastructure, a healthcare professional who improves community wellbeing, a researcher who generates new evidence, a surveyor who supports sustainable development or a technology entrepreneur who creates jobs.

 

Others may apply STEM-related skills to agriculture, climate action, education, communication or environmental management. The ultimate value of STEM empowerment is not limited to the number of girls reached; it is also reflected in the choices they become confident enough to make and the solutions they may create in the future.

 

A Completed Project with Lasting Significance

 

Although the STEM Empowerment Project was completed on 23 February 2026, its significance extends beyond the completion date. The encouragement, exposure and sense of possibility created through the initiative can continue to influence the participants as they progress through their education.

 

Project completion represents the achievement of a defined intervention, but it does not end TIJCEF’s commitment to promoting girls’ education and leadership. Instead, it provides a foundation for strengthening future initiatives and reaching more girls in other schools and communities.

 

The completion of the project also demonstrates TIJCEF’s commitment to implementing practical interventions with clearly identified beneficiaries, locations and outcomes. Reaching 400 girls at Government Girls’ School, Yola, represents a measurable contribution to the Foundation’s broader goal of expanding opportunities for women and girls.

 

Investing in Girls’ Agency

 

Investing in girls’ agency benefits entire communities. Girls who are educated, confident and empowered to make informed decisions are better positioned to participate in leadership, innovation and economic development.

 

As technology continues to transform education, healthcare, agriculture, environmental management and employment, girls must be prepared to participate not only as users of technology but also as creators, researchers and decision-makers.

 

The completed STEM Empowerment Project at Government Girls’ School, Yola, reflects TIJCEF’s determination to ensure that girls are not left behind. By reaching 400 students, the Foundation created an opportunity for the participants to see STEM as accessible and their ambitions as achievable.

 

The project stands as an important milestone under TIJCEF’s Agency Pillar. It demonstrates how targeted educational interventions can strengthen girls’ confidence, expand their awareness of future opportunities and encourage them to take greater ownership of their educational and professional journeys.

 

Through initiatives of this nature, TIJCEF continues to advance a future in which women and girls have the knowledge, voice, confidence and opportunities required to make choices, pursue their aspirations and contribute meaningfully to society.

TIJCEF, Lead the Girl Foundation Empower 200 Girls at Adroit International Academy Yola

TIJCEF, Lead the Girl Foundation Empower 200 Girls at Adroit International Academy Yola

 

The Tijwun Care and Empowerment Foundation (TIJCEF), in partnership with Lead the Girl Foundation, has carried out a girls’ empowerment programme at Adroit International Academy in Yola, Adamawa State, reaching 200 girls as part of efforts to strengthen confidence, personal development and awareness of opportunities among young girls.

 

The school-based intervention brought the two organisations directly into an educational environment where they engaged the students on issues connected to their development and future.

 

According to programme records, 200 girls participated in the outreach, providing a documented beneficiary figure for the intervention and making it one of TIJCEF’s girls-focused activities in Yola.

 

The programme aligns with TIJCEF’s Dignity pillar, through which the Foundation promotes the principle that girls and other beneficiaries should not simply receive assistance but should be recognised as individuals with abilities, aspirations and the potential to contribute meaningfully to their communities.

 

The collaboration with Lead the Girl Foundation also placed partnership at the centre of the intervention, demonstrating how civil society organisations can combine their platforms and experience to reach young people within schools.

 

200 Girls Reached Through Joint Intervention

 

At Adroit International Academy, the focus was on the girls themselves.

 

Rather than organising a broad community event where the target population could be difficult to determine, the school setting enabled TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation to work with a clearly identified group.

 

By the end of the intervention, 200 girls had been reached.

 

The figure is significant to TIJCEF’s reporting because it represents the number of direct participants rather than an estimated indirect audience.

 

For the Foundation, the outreach added to its growing engagement with girls and young people in Adamawa State and reinforced its commitment to bringing development programmes closer to beneficiaries within their everyday environments.

 

Schools are particularly important locations for this type of intervention because they provide opportunities to engage girls during a period when many are developing their educational ambitions, confidence and ideas about future careers.

 

Partnership Drives the Yola Outreach

 

The programme was jointly undertaken by TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation, making collaboration an important part of the intervention.

 

Both organisations worked together to reach the girls at Adroit International Academy rather than the activity being implemented by TIJCEF alone.

 

For community-based organisations, partnerships can help extend the reach of programmes while bringing different experiences and approaches into a single intervention.

 

The Adroit programme provides a practical example of this approach.

 

It also demonstrates the role schools can play as partners in community development. By providing access to students in an organised learning environment, educational institutions can serve as platforms through which civil society organisations deliver complementary programmes on leadership, personal development, health, skills and other issues affecting young people.

 

Wider Evidence Shows Why Girls-Focused Programmes Matter

 

The intervention in Yola took place against a wider national environment in which millions of Nigerian girls and adolescents continue to face challenges affecting education, skills development and their transition into adulthood.

 

Nigeria has nearly 105 million children and adolescents aged 0–17, representing about half of the country’s population, according to the Federal Government and UNICEF’s updated situation analysis. The scale means that investments in children and adolescents have major implications for Nigeria’s future human capital.

 

Recent evidence also demonstrates that girls can face barriers extending beyond access to a classroom.

 

UNICEF’s research on adolescent girls in northern Nigeria identified social and gender norms, child marriage, adolescent pregnancy and restrictions around digital participation among factors capable of limiting girls’ education and development. The research also identified skills development, mentorship, role models and community engagement among approaches that can strengthen opportunities for girls.

 

While the research focused particularly on north-western Nigeria, it illustrates the broader importance of ensuring that girls have opportunities to develop skills, interact with role models and participate in programmes that expand their understanding of what is possible.

 

The Adroit International Academy programme represents a grassroots contribution to that broader development objective within Adamawa State.

 

Skills Development Is Becoming Increasingly Important

 

Girls’ empowerment is also increasingly connected to skills development.

 

UNICEF reported that close to 590,000 Nigerian children developed technical, vocational and foundational skills in 2025, including more than 270,000 girls.

 

The scale of these national programmes is far beyond that of a grassroots organisation such as TIJCEF, but the comparison demonstrates why local interventions remain relevant.

 

Large national programmes can reach hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries, while smaller organisations can work directly within individual schools and communities.

 

TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation’s engagement with 200 girls represents this local approach.

 

It allows interventions to reach students within their immediate environment while creating opportunities for future relationships between schools and civil society organisations.

 

Dignity at the Centre of the Programme

 

The Adroit intervention is classified under TIJCEF’s Dignity pillar because the Foundation’s approach to dignity extends beyond the distribution of material assistance.

 

For TIJCEF, dignity includes recognising that young girls have ambitions and abilities that deserve encouragement and development.

 

The 200 students reached through the programme were therefore not treated merely as statistics or recipients.

 

They were the central participants in the intervention.

 

This approach is consistent with emerging evidence on adolescent-girl programming.

 

UNICEF’s research with girls and communities in northern Nigeria found that adolescent girls themselves identified access to skills, female role models, education and greater inclusion as important elements of their development.

 

Such findings strengthen the case for programmes that create direct engagement with girls rather than designing interventions without their participation.

 

Reporting the Impact Responsibly

 

For TIJCEF, the most clearly documented result of the Adroit International Academy programme is its reach of 200 girls.

 

The Foundation is not presenting unsupported percentages claiming that confidence, academic performance or career aspirations increased by a particular amount because such outcomes would require specific baseline and follow-up measurements.

 

Instead, the programme provides a verified record of a girls-focused intervention delivered through partnership at a school in Yola.

 

This distinction is important to TIJCEF’s approach to evidence-based reporting.

 

Photographs and programme documentation can establish that an activity took place. Attendance or beneficiary records can establish the number reached. More complex claims about behavioural or educational change require additional evidence.

 

By separating these levels of evidence, TIJCEF can report its work without exaggerating its achievements.

 

A Contribution to Girls’ Development in Adamawa

 

The challenges facing Nigerian girls are too extensive for any single organisation to address.

 

Government remains responsible for ensuring access to quality education and creating policies that protect and expand opportunities for children. Schools, families, civil society organisations, communities and development partners also have important roles.

 

The intervention at Adroit International Academy represents TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation’s contribution at the grassroots level.

 

For the school, it brought an additional girls-focused development activity directly to students.

 

For the two organisations, it provided an opportunity to translate their commitment to girls’ empowerment into direct engagement.

 

Most importantly, 200 girls participated.

 

That number represents 200 individual students reached through the programme rather than an abstract development statistic.

 

As TIJCEF continues its community interventions, the Adroit International Academy programme provides documented evidence of how partnership can translate organisational values into practical action.

 

The programme also reinforces the Foundation’s Dignity pillar: the belief that every girl should be recognised not simply according to the challenges she faces, but according to the potential she possesses.

 

For TIJCEF and Lead the Girl Foundation, reaching 200 girls in Yola was one practical contribution towards creating that opportunity.

About the Grant

Implementation research focuses on understanding how proven or promising health interventions can be delivered more effectively in real-world settings.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on laboratory discoveries, implementation research examines practical questions surrounding health systems, service delivery, access, adoption and effectiveness.

This makes the programme particularly relevant to researchers and institutions working directly with communities and health systems.

The 2026–2027 call seeks proposals addressing priority public health issues within the WHO African Region.

Funding Available

Successful projects may receive up to US$15,000.

The relatively focused grant size makes the programme suitable for implementation research projects capable of producing practical evidence within a defined period.

Who Can Apply?

The official call is restricted to applicants from eligible countries within the WHO African Region. Nigeria is among the eligible countries identified for the opportunity.

The opportunity is particularly relevant to universities, research institutions, health-related organisations and qualified researchers capable of undertaking implementation research.

NGOs interested in the opportunity should verify their exact institutional eligibility rather than assuming that all registered civil society organisations automatically qualify.

Why Implementation Research Matters

Many African countries have health policies and interventions with strong potential, but implementation challenges can limit their effectiveness.

These barriers may include shortages of trained personnel, weak infrastructure, low community participation, geographical inequalities, poor access to information, inadequate data and difficulties translating national policies into effective local services.

Implementation research can help identify why such gaps exist and test practical approaches to addressing them.

For community-focused organisations, this can create opportunities to connect local experience with scientific evidence and policy improvement.

Developing a Strong Proposal

Applicants should start with a clearly defined implementation problem rather than an overly broad health topic.

For example, instead of proposing general research on maternal health, an applicant could investigate why women in a particular underserved area are not accessing an established maternal-health intervention and evaluate practical strategies for improving uptake.

Similarly, researchers could investigate implementation barriers affecting disease surveillance, digital health interventions, community health programmes or other regional priorities identified in the official call.

A competitive proposal should demonstrate the importance of the implementation problem, explain the research methodology, identify expected outcomes and show how findings could contribute to improved health practice or policy.
